item.title: Belvedere rejects Mallard Pointe permit appeal after four-hour hearing
item.description: The Belvedere City Council unanimously rejected a residents group’s appeal of Mallard Pointe’s bulkhead permits Nov. 9, finding paperwork errors but no reason to overturn them.
item.content:encoded:
The Belvedere City Council unanimously rejected a residents group’s appeal of Mallard Pointe’s bulkhead permits Nov. 9, finding paperwork errors but no reason to overturn them.

The Belvedere City Council unanimously rejected a residents group’s challenge to Mallard Pointe’s bulkhead permits Nov. 9, ending a heavily attended four-hour afternoon hearing in which members acknowledged paperwork errors but found no basis to overturn the approvals.

The council first voted 4-1 to deny a request by Belvedere Residents for Intelligent Growth, or BRIG, to postpone the hearing, with Councilmember Jane Cooper dissenting. BRIG wanted to keep the appeal open through the winter, arguing the rains of a predicted El Niño season would show how construction along the lagoon shoreline was holding up.

All five members then voted to deny the appeal, leaving intact two permits issued Oct. 1 to replace about 900 feet of shoreline bulkheads. The work includes removing the old walls, driving vinyl sheet piles into the lagoon bed and excavating and backfilling behind them.

item.title: First of three Bay Area storms arrives Friday with rain, gusts and flood-prone tide
item.description: A coastal flood advisory covers the Tiburon Peninsula shoreline until 4 p.m. Nov. 13 as the first of three storms brings rain and gusts that could top 45 mph.
item.content:encoded:
A coastal flood advisory covers the Tiburon Peninsula shoreline until 4 p.m. Nov. 13 as the first of three storms brings rain and gusts that could top 45 mph.

The midday high tide Nov. 13 could flood Tiburon’s lowest shoreline streets just as the first of three storms forecast over the next week reaches the Bay Area with rain, gusts that could top 45 mph and a chance of thunderstorms.

The National Weather Service’s coastal flood advisory for the bay shoreline, including Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry, runs until 4 p.m. Nov. 13 and warns of up to 1.5 feet of water in low-lying areas.

NOAA tide predictions and recent gauge readings put that high tide off Tiburon at about 1:15 p.m., when water could reach Greenwood Beach Road and Tiburon Boulevard at Beach Road. The Beach Road intersection flooded Oct. 11 on a dry day.

The tide could test the wooden “tide boxes” Tiburon Public Works crews built over downtown storm drains to keep bay water from backing up onto the streets. The town has said crews pull the boxes whenever it rains so the drains can carry runoff, and residents should then expect flooding in those spots depending on rainfall and tides.

Rain is forecast to pick up across the North Bay from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. Nov. 13, with up to 1.25 inches in its coastal hills and 0.3-0.8 inch around San Francisco Bay by the afternoon of Nov. 14. Southerly gusts of 25-35 mph the night of Nov. 12 could top 45 mph just ahead of the cold front, strong enough to down trees and knock out power in spots, according to the weather service.

Boaters on the bay north of the Bay Bridge face a small craft advisory from 9 p.m. Nov. 12 to 9 a.m. 13, then a gale warning until 3 p.m.

Two more storms follow, Nov. 15-16 and again around the middle of next week, though forecasters don’t expect either to stall over one area, and early forecasts don’t show either bringing much more rain than the first.

The weekend’s big-surf warnings cover the Pacific coast from Point Reyes south through San Francisco and Monterey Bay to Big Sur, where breaking waves of 25 to 35 feet are forecast from the evening of Nov. 13 to early Nov. 15, with occasional 40- to 50-foot sets at some breaks. Waves could also wash over seawalls and run up beaches into low-lying areas Nov. 14, and the weather service calls the risk of drowning very high.

item.title: Belvedere parks panel makes Cliff Lane path to the shore its 2027 focus
item.description: Belvedere’s parks and lanes committee wants to restore Cliff Lane, an unmarked public path from Beach Road to a pocket beach, as its main focus in 2027.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere’s parks and lanes committee wants to restore Cliff Lane, an unmarked public path from Beach Road to a pocket beach, as its main focus in 2027.

Cliff Lane, an unmarked public path from Beach Road down to a pocket beach, would be the Belvedere Parks, Open Spaces and Lanes Committee’s main focus in 2027 under a draft list of priorities presented by its chair.

Chair Charlie Harrington proposed the focus at the committee’s Nov. 3 special meeting. The list also calls for continuing the conversation about Centennial Park once its wooden stairs are repaired and taking a closer look at improvements to Belvedere Way.

Harrington said he would bring a draft of the committee’s annual letter to the City Council to its next meeting. The priorities are expected to go to the council early next year.

item.title: Tiburon crews box in downtown drains to keep tidewater off streets
item.description: Tiburon Public Works crews built wooden tide boxes over downtown storm drains to keep high tides from backing up onto Beach Road and other low-lying streets.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon Public Works crews built wooden tide boxes over downtown storm drains to keep high tides from backing up onto Beach Road and other low-lying streets.

Tiburon Public Works crews have built wooden “tide boxes” over storm drains at low-lying downtown intersections to keep high tides from backing up onto the streets.

The boxes sit at Beach Road’s intersections with Tiburon Boulevard and Juanita Lane and at other spots that flood at high tide, according to a Nov. 2 town newsletter.

Each box sits over a drain. As the tide rises and pushes bay water up through the pipes, the box traps it and keeps it out of the street. The water recedes as the tide falls, the newsletter said. Crews seal the seams and hold each box down with weighted bags.

item.content:encoded:
Tiburon resident Jill Dallas, out walking her dog, Lilo, talks about the waterfront, trails and familiar faces that have kept her in town for four years.

On Nov. 4, Tiburon resident Jill Dallas is out walking her dog, Lilo, who rubs against the legs of passersby while Dallas talks about the town she has called home for four years.

Her partner brought her north from Los Altos Hills. The waterfront, the nearby trails and the faces she knows around town have kept her here.

“I love it up here,” Dallas says. “I love being close to the water and closer to the city.”

item.title: Tiburon launches $100,000 pilot to share costs of private drain repairs
item.description: Tiburon will pay property owners up to half the cost, capped at $25,000, to fix failing private culverts and drain pipes under a $100,000 pilot approved Nov. 4.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon will pay property owners up to half the cost, capped at $25,000, to fix failing private culverts and drain pipes under a $100,000 pilot approved Nov. 4.

Tiburon will pay property owners up to half the cost, capped at $25,000, to fix failing private culverts and storm-drain pipes whose collapse could flood streets, damage town infrastructure or threaten public safety.

The Town Council approved the 12-month pilot program unanimously on Nov. 4. The program sets aside $100,000 and also covers catch basins, energy dissipators, drainage channels and other drainage structures approved by the Public Works Department.

Individual owners, neighbors applying jointly, homeowners associations, common-interest developments and other private owners can apply, and every owner of record must sign. The town will take applications for 12 months, and each approved project then has 12 months to finish.

item.title: Richardson Bay Sanitary District incumbents win new terms
item.description: Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens will keep their Richardson Bay Sanitary District seats over challenger John Turnacliff.
item.content:encoded:
Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens will keep their Richardson Bay Sanitary District seats over challenger John Turnacliff.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens will win new four-year terms on the Richardson Bay Sanitary District board, holding off challenger John Turnacliff in the count the county posted Nov. 9. The three would serve through November 2030, joining sitting board members Mark Slater and Jeff Slavitz.

Fitzgerald had votes on 47.4% of ballots counted, McIntosh on 46.2%, Walravens on 45.8% and Turnacliff on 19% in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9. Voters could choose up to three candidates, so the shares add up to more than 100%.

When those returns posted, 91,634 ballots had been counted countywide, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The results are unofficial. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16 and gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results. The county plans updates Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over a missing or mismatched signature, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix the problem.

The district’s first contested election since 2018 came amid renewed debate over whether Marin’s sanitary districts should consolidate. The board voted unanimously July 21 to reject all seven findings and nine recommendations in a Marin civil grand jury report that urged special districts to explore consolidation. District officials argued that the report failed to account for existing joint operations or the financial risks of merging.

The incumbents largely defended the district’s operations during preelection interviews with The Ark. Fitzgerald, a Tiburon Fire Protection District captain and the son of Ark contract bookkeeper Marion Fitzgerald and her husband, Jim, emphasized preparing for staff turnover and maintaining fiscal discipline.

McIntosh, the board president and co-founder of environmental-sensor company EnviroSmarts, stressed keeping sewer-service charges low and maintaining regional partnerships.

Walravens, a financial analyst and former attorney, pointed to financial stewardship and support for maintenance and capital improvements. All three said they doubted consolidation would improve the district’s service or finances, and Mark Fitzgerald and Walravens left room to consider specific efficiencies.

Turnacliff, who owns Golden Gate Equipment Finance and chairs the Marin County Republican Central Committee, said he would bring experience in financing, equipment planning and financial oversight. He said he was open to studying consolidation if it made financial and operational sense.

The district serves northern Tiburon from Gilmartin Drive to Highway 101 and all of Strawberry. It collects wastewater and pumps it to Mill Valley for treatment through the Sewerage Agency of Southern Marin.

The election was Fitzgerald’s first appearance on the ballot after more than four years on the board.

“For it to come to the voters and choose me amongst the other two, I’m thankful,” he said.

Looking ahead, Fitzgerald said his role includes overseeing how the district manages current spending and plans for future expenses.

“That’s what I care most about is that they plan for the future, spend money wisely currently and forecast the future cost,” he said.

Fitzgerald also praised McIntosh’s leadership as board president and said the board would revisit its officer assignments.

“Future outlook is just keep running a good agency,” he said.

McIntosh said the board’s work in the coming months would be routine, with no major votes scheduled. The district will review its accounting and business practices as it closes out the year, he said.

“It literally is business as usual,” McIntosh said. “We just kind of check everything to make sure we’re on track and we’re staying at or below budget.”

Turnacliff said in an email that the race was his first run for public office and that he thanked the voters who supported him.

“I’m a little disappointed, but I’m glad I ran and congratulations to the winners,” he said.

He said he plans to run again, “maybe for this seat, maybe another.”

item.title: Saghezchi, Waterfield, Teese keep Strawberry Rec board seats
item.description: Incumbents Sohrab Saghezchi, Sarah Waterfield and Peter Teese will win four-year Strawberry Recreation District seats over challenger David Morgenthaler.
item.content:encoded:
Incumbents Sohrab Saghezchi, Sarah Waterfield and Peter Teese will win four-year Strawberry Recreation District seats over challenger David Morgenthaler.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Incumbents Sohrab Saghezchi, Sarah Waterfield and board Chair Peter Teese will win the three four-year seats on the Strawberry Recreation District board, holding off challenger David Morgenthaler in the count the county posted Nov. 9.

Waterfield did not publicly campaign or sit for an interview, and in an email she declined to say whether she would take the seat.

Saghezchi had votes on 44.6% of ballots counted, Waterfield on 42.2%, Teese on 36.5% and Morgenthaler on 32.1% in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9. Voters could choose up to three candidates, so the shares add up to more than 100%.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

In a separate race for the board’s one two-year seat, appointed incumbent Doug Twillman is projected to win, with 65.9% of the vote to challenger Aliza Hawkins’ 34.1%.

When the Nov. 9 returns posted, 91,634 ballots had been counted countywide, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. The results are unofficial. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16 and gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results. The county plans updates Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over a missing or mismatched signature, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix the problem.

Morgenthaler, a Strawberry resident, mounted a rare challenge in a district that often struggles to draw candidates. Teese was elected without opposition in 2014, 2018 and 2022.

Teese, a board member since December 2010, sought a fifth term. Saghezchi, a Mill Valley dentist whom county supervisors appointed in December 2022 after no one filed for the seat, sought election to it for the first time. Waterfield joined the board in December 2024 after running uncontested for a shortened two-year term.

Morgenthaler, a sales professional and musician, campaigned on expanding programs for teenagers and adding offerings such as foreign-language and music classes. Saghezchi emphasized transparency, fiscal responsibility and community involvement, while Teese said his top priority was completing the district’s planned playground.

The incoming board will oversee a district serving about 6,000 residents in unincorporated Strawberry, with year-round recreation programs, classes, memberships and events.

Among its major projects is a playground planned for the grass between the tennis courts and baseball fields at Strawberry Park. The contractor, GameTime, trimmed the design to about $2.55 million in October, restroom included, and the board scheduled a final vote for Nov. 10, after The Ark’s press deadline. The district plans to break ground in 2027.

Saghezchi said he was “thrilled and honored” to continue serving the community and grateful for Strawberry residents’ support. He said he saw the results as an encouraging sign that residents recognized the board’s work.

Looking ahead to 2027, Saghezchi said he wants to continue improving the district’s facilities and programs and find more ways to bring residents together.

“Strawberry is a magical place, and I’m incredibly proud to call it home,” he said.

Teese said he was grateful, though he found it difficult to draw broader conclusions from the results beyond what he saw as an advantage for incumbents.

“I was happy to be in the top three,” he said.

“It’s a funny and odd reminder of democracy at work,” Teese said of seeing voters assign a number to each candidate.

He said a fifth term would be his last. The district has no term limits. The board voted unanimously Aug. 18 to reject a Marin civil grand jury recommendation that special districts cap members at two consecutive four-year terms.

Teese said the playground project would require a separate bidding process for site excavation, rather than handling that work and the playground equipment as a single package, and that the board would take up the excavation bidding Nov. 10.

Teese characterized the additional bidding requirement as an added step, not a complication, but expressed frustration with the government procedures involved in moving the project forward.

“Just to do a community good,” he said, “the legal hurdles that you face from your own team are astonishing.”

“I feel great about the playground, and I feel like an underdog when it comes to being up against red tape and bureaucracy and just the inertia of the state,” he said.

Morgenthaler said he expected the three incumbents to win reelection, though he stopped short of conceding as votes continued to be counted.

“I expect that the three incumbents will be reelected,” he said. “That’s my expectation at this point.”

Morgenthaler, who was making his first run for the board, called the current board “very capable” and said he planned to keep attending meetings. He also expressed interest in seeking an appointment if a seat opens before the next election.

“In the event that there is a vacancy in between now and the next cycle, I anticipate that I will show up and raise my hand,” he said.

Morgenthaler said he was “somewhat better than cautiously optimistic” about the district’s planned playground and would keep following its fundraising progress.

“I am very optimistic that the playground will be a wonderful way of expanding (the district’s) reach across the entire community,” he said.

Appointed incumbent Doug Twillman had 65.9% of the vote to Aliza Hawkins’ 34.1% for a two-year Strawberry Recreation District seat in the Nov. 9 count.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Appointed incumbent Doug Twillman is projected to win a two-year seat on the Strawberry Recreation District board, taking about two-thirds of the vote in the count the county posted Nov. 9 against challenger Aliza Hawkins, who sought the same seat by appointment last year.

Twillman had 65.9% of the vote to Hawkins’ 34.1% in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9, when 91,634 ballots had been counted countywide, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters.

The results are unofficial.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16 and gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results. The county plans updates Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over a missing or mismatched signature, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix the problem.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

Twillman said his focus now is making sure the district builds its major new playground, slated for 2027.

“I’m excited, but I’ve never run in the interest of being popular,” he said. “I got a lot of eyes on me to make sure we get the playground done right.”

Hawkins did not respond to requests for comment.

The candidates competed for a single two-year seat in a rare contested election for a district that has historically struggled to attract candidates. Their campaigns emphasized community engagement, financial oversight and the future of the district’s planned playground.

Twillman joined the board in September 2025, when members selected him over Hawkins on a 3-1 vote to replace Cale Nichols, who had moved out of state. Board member Sohrab Saghezchi cast the dissenting vote, favoring Hawkins. The election put that choice before voters.

A financial analyst and consultant with more than 30 years of experience, Twillman emphasized fiscal oversight and completing the playground at Strawberry Park. He serves on the board’s fundraising committee for the project and called for dependable cost estimates before construction commitments.

“The budget should be well understood so that we can hold the contractors accountable and the community can hold us accountable for a successful physical and fiscal outcome,” Twillman said during the campaign.

Hawkins, whose background includes marketing, advertising and counseling, focused on increasing participation in district programs and helping residents feel included and represented.

“I would love to see more community engagement as well, just even letting people know more of what we have going on,” Hawkins said during the campaign.

A mother of two whose family regularly uses the district’s pool, programs and recreation facilities, Hawkins said she wanted the district to serve residents at every stage of life.

Playground company GameTime trimmed the design to about $2.55 million in October, restroom included. The board scheduled a final vote for Nov. 10, after The Ark’s press deadline. The district plans to break ground in 2027.

Established in 1949, the independent district serves about 6,000 residents in unincorporated areas of Mill Valley and Tiburon east of Highway 101. It operates the recreation center and maintains four parks, a public dock, walking trails and the Water Tank Hill open space.

item.title: Paradise Cay’s Measure Z dredging tax extension set to pass
item.description: Paradise Cay’s Measure Z, extending the parcel tax that pays to dredge its canals and channels, had 84.1% support in the county’s Nov. 9 count.
item.content:encoded:
Paradise Cay’s Measure Z, extending the parcel tax that pays to dredge its canals and channels, had 84.1% support in the county’s Nov. 9 count.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Paradise Cay’s Measure Z is projected to pass, extending the special parcel tax that pays to dredge the community’s canals and the two channels connecting it to San Francisco Bay.

The measure won 116 votes, or 84.1%, to 22 votes, or 15.9%, in the Marin County Elections Department’s count posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9. It needed two-thirds of the votes cast to pass.

The results are unofficial. As of Nov. 9, the county had counted 91,634 ballots, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16 and gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results. The county plans updates Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over a missing or mismatched signature, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix the problem.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

“We’re of course relieved that it passed and still by a decent margin,” said Eric Lyons, who chairs the six-member advisory board of County Service Area No. 29, the county-run district that collects the tax. “But it’s a little disappointing that there were 21 members who voted no.”

Lyons said some voters may have objected to the $300 increase.

“Of course costs are always going up. But we didn’t hear any pushback from anybody about that really in our little surveys,” he said. “But there are some older folks in the neighborhood that probably just would love to avoid any additional taxes on their bill, but I think we just probably need a little better education on what it really means.”

He said the district needs to better explain that a “no” vote would end the tax rather than keep the previous rate. If the tax lapsed, the community would lose its dedicated source of dredging money, which Lyons has said keeps the canals clear for boating and recreation.

“Without a yes vote, we don’t collect any money anymore,” he said.

Paradise Cay was built along the Tiburon Peninsula as a waterfront community organized around a network of residential canals. Keeping those canals and the entrances to the bay navigable requires the periodic removal of sediment carried into the waterways.

The waterways were last dredged in 2020 and 2024, and the community typically needs dredging every four or five years, depending on how quickly sediment accumulates.

The next dredging project is tentatively expected in 2028, Lyons said. Depending on conditions, the district might be able to wait until 2029.

“Our forecast shows that should be sufficient for 4-5 year dredging episodes over the next 10 years, but the cost of dredging and associated ‘soft’ costs (permits, planning and testing) has been rising rapidly, so we can only hope,” he said in September.

The 2024 project cost more than $1 million, including permits, planning, testing and other soft costs, Lyons said.

Measure Z would raise the tax in the service area from $1,900 per lot this year to $2,200 beginning July 1, 2027. The rate would rise automatically by 3% each year starting July 1, 2028, and the tax would expire June 30, 2037. With those increases, it would reach about $2,870 a lot in its final year.

The service area estimates the measure would raise an average of about $272,800 a year for maintenance dredging in Paradise Cay’s principal waterways and the north and south entry channels. The tax applies to lots in the district, which covers the Paradise Cay parcels with canal access rather than the whole neighborhood. The money may be used only for the purposes stated in the measure.

Measure Z would continue the existing parcel tax, which is scheduled to expire June 30, 2027. The current tax is Paradise Cay’s 2016 Measure O, which voters approved with 87.2% of the vote. It set a $1,500 annual parcel tax that could rise as much as 3% a year, to a maximum of $1,950 by 2026.

Measure O replaced a $1,200 annual parcel tax that 93.8% of voters approved in 2007. Measure Z’s 84.1% is the lowest yes vote of the three.

Jackie Elward is projected to beat Supervisor Eric Lucan for the peninsula’s Assembly seat, while the billionaire tax trailed statewide and locally.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Rohnert Park Councilmember Jackie Elward is projected to win the Assembly seat representing the peninsula over Marin Supervisor Eric Lucan, while a one-time tax on billionaires trailed statewide and by even wider margins in Tiburon and Belvedere.

At the top of the ballot, Democrat Xavier Becerra will win the race for governor over Republican Steve Hilton, with a nearly 2-1 majority.

All results are unofficial and will change. The secretary of state’s 2:21 p.m. Nov. 9 update showed all 23,860 of the state’s precincts reporting, but Marin and other counties are still counting ballots.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

Marin’s Nov. 9 update counted 91,634 ballots, about 52.7% of the county’s 173,804 registered voters. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16.

Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over missing or mismatched signatures, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them. The county plans updates Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25, and state law gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

On the peninsula, the county had counted ballots from 3,838 of Tiburon’s 7,553 registered voters, or 50.8%; 785 of Belvedere’s 1,618, or 48.5%; and 1,615 of Strawberry’s 3,081, or 52.4%. Peninsula figures are The Ark’s tallies of the precincts serving Belvedere, Strawberry and Tiburon, including unincorporated Tiburon areas such as Paradise Cay.

Results for the local council, school and district races and Paradise Cay’s Measure Z run in separate stories.

Special district, Strawberry and northern Tiburon voters

All four incumbents will win the four seats on the Southern Marin Fire Protection District board: Cristine Soto DeBerry with votes on 46.2% of ballots counted, Kurt Chun with 44.5%, Thomas Perazzo with 38.4% and Peter Fleming of Strawberry with 37.4%. Challengers Eric Steinhofer, 26.3%; Amy Svendberg, 24.7%; and Thomas Clark, 7.2%, trailed.

Belvedere Councilmembers Jane Cooper and Peter Mark, the only candidates for two seats, had votes on 71.5% and 63.3% of ballots counted. Incumbents also ran unopposed for three other boards: Joy Ho, Rick Jones and Cheryl Woodford on the Tiburon Fire Protection District board; Catharine Benediktsson and Tod Moody on the Sanitary District No. 5 of Marin board; and Natalie Katz, Sharon Nakatani and Yunhee Yoo on the board of the Mill Valley School District, which serves Strawberry Point Elementary School.

Ho, Woodford and Jones are scheduled to take the oath of office at the Tiburon Fire board’s meeting at 4 Nov. 11.

Marin County and Marin Healthcare District special taxes, all voters; each qualified by petition and needs a simple majority

Measure CC, the Marin Healthcare District’s 30-year parcel tax of 14 cents per square foot of building space for intensive care, trauma, emergency and other hospital capacity, will pass with 56.7%. It led in all three peninsula communities, with 53.8% in Tiburon, 51.4% in Belvedere and 56.5% in Strawberry.

The district estimates the tax will raise about $12.4 million a year to expand and modernize intensive care, trauma, triage and patient rooms at MarinHealth Medical Center and to hire and keep doctors and nurses. None of it can go to administrators’ salaries. It has no exemption for seniors or low-income owners, and the district may borrow against it. Opponents noted that district taxpayers are still paying off the $394 million hospital bond voters approved in 2013.

Measure P, the county’s 15-year childcare parcel tax of 5 cents per square foot, is projected to pass with 54.2%, though Tiburon voted against it 52.7% to 47.3% and Belvedere 55.7% to 44.3%. Strawberry backed it with 54.8%.

The county estimates the tax will raise about $12.5 million a year for childcare and preschool for low- and middle-income families, raises for childcare workers and new or improved childcare facilities, with no more than 5% for administration. The Marin County Children and Families Commission will write a five-year spending plan, and supervisors may raise the rate each year with inflation. Like Measure CC, it has no exemption for seniors or low-income owners.

Federal and state officials, district voters

Elward is projected to win the race to succeed Assemblymember Damon Connolly, D-San Rafael, in the 12th Assembly District, leading Lucan 56.6% to 43.4% with all 301 of its precincts reporting. Elward also led in Marin, 53.9% to 46.1%.

The peninsula went the other way. Lucan carried Tiburon with 56.5% and Belvedere with 64.3%, while Elward took Strawberry, 53.8% to 46.2%.

Connolly will win the open 2nd District state Senate seat over Republican Tief Gibbs of Novato, leading 74.7% to 25.3%.

Rep. Jared Huffman, D-San Rafael, will win reelection over Republican Robin Littau of Redding, leading 64.6% to 35.4% across the 2nd Congressional District. He took 82.9% in Marin.

State officials, all voters

Becerra will win with 65.6% to Hilton’s 34.4% in the secretary of state’s Nov. 9 count. He took 79.7% in Marin, 69.8% in Tiburon, 64.2% in Belvedere and 78% in Strawberry. Hilton, a former Fox News host from Atherton, ran best on the peninsula in Belvedere, at 35.8%.

Democrats will win the other partisan statewide races by similar margins: Treasurer Fiona Ma over Republican Gloria Romero for lieutenant governor, 65.5% to 34.5%; Secretary of State Shirley Weber over Republican Don Wagner, 66.5% to 33.5%; Controller Malia Cohen over Republican Herb Morgan, 65.5% to 34.5%; Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis over Republican Jennifer Hawks for treasurer, 65.7% to 34.3%; and Attorney General Rob Bonta over Republican Michael Gates, 65.5% to 34.5%.

The closest statewide race, for insurance commissioner, pitted two Democrats. Jane Kim is projected to win over state Sen. Ben Allen, leading 53.5% to 46.5%. Allen carried Marin with 56.3% and ran stronger still on the peninsula, with 64.5% in Tiburon, 68.8% in Belvedere and 62.1% in Strawberry.

In the nonpartisan race for superintendent of public instruction, San Diego Unified board President Richard Barrera will win over Chino Valley Unified board President Sonja Shaw, leading 58.9% to 41.1%. Barrera took 69.4% in Marin, 61.7% in Tiburon, 59.7% in Belvedere and 68.2% in Strawberry.

For the Board of Equalization’s District 2 seat, incumbent Sally Lieber will win over fellow Democrat John Pimentel, leading 59.9% to 40.1%.

All voters; each needs a simple majority

Proposition 40, the one-time 5% tax on the wealth of billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026, trailed with 53.2% voting no statewide and 53.9% no in Marin. Tiburon voted against it 68.2% to 31.8% and Belvedere 77.8% to 22.2%. Strawberry opposed it 57.1% to 42.9%.

Proposition 42, one of two measures written to block it, led 52% to 48%. It would bar new state taxes on owning retirement accounts, financial assets and other personal property. Tiburon and Belvedere backed it, and Marin and Strawberry opposed it.

The other, Proposition 41, is projected to fail, trailing 45.4% to 54.6%. It would bar collecting any new tax that, like Proposition 40’s revenue, is exempt from the state spending limit. Belvedere backed it 56.3% to 43.7%, and Tiburon narrowly opposed it, 50.4% to 49.6%.

Proposition 3, which would make permanent the top income-tax brackets voters approved in 2012 and extended in 2016, will pass. It led 60.4% to 39.6% statewide and drew 67.3% in Marin. Tiburon narrowly opposed it, 51.6% to 48.4%, and Belvedere voted against it 59.5% to 40.5%. Strawberry backed it with 64.4%.

Proposition 5 is projected to pass, leading 51.9% to 48.1%, a margin of about 377,000 votes out of about 10 million. It would drop the replacement-candidate question from recall ballots and let the lieutenant governor succeed a recalled governor. Marin backed it with 58.9%, while Tiburon and Belvedere were narrowly against.

Proposition 38, the $8.4 billion immunology research bond, will pass. It had 54.3% statewide but trailed narrowly in Marin, 42,462 votes to 42,388, and in Tiburon and Belvedere.

Proposition 4, the closest measure on the ballot, would lift the state’s ban on public financing of campaigns. It trailed 49.6% to 50.4%, though Marin backed it with 56.4%.

Proposition 1, the $11.25 billion housing and veterans bond, passed with 60.9% to 39.1% and drew 68.4% in Marin. Proposition 2, which would double the cap on the state’s rainy-day fund, also passed. It had 61.2% and drew 73% in Marin. Proposition 37, the middle-income homebuyer loan program, passed with 62.2% and drew 65.2% in Marin.

Proposition 39, requiring voter ID, failed. It trailed 39.6% to 60.4%, and 76.5% of Marin voters opposed it. Proposition 43, which would require two-thirds approval for citizen-initiated local special taxes starting Jan. 1, 2027, will fail, trailing 43% to 57%, with 65.5% of Marin voters opposed.

Proposition 44, requiring community health clinics to spend at least 90% of revenue on patient care, failed. It trailed 17.9% to 82.1%, and 86.6% of Marin voters opposed it. Proposition 45, a faster environmental-review track for housing, infrastructure and other projects, is projected to fail, trailing 44.1% to 55.9%, and 71.4% of Marin voters opposed it.

California Supreme Court Associate Justices Kelli Evans and Joshua Groban will win retention to new 12-year terms, with 72.5% and 71.5% voting yes statewide.

item.title: Antani extends lead over Godfrey for third Reed board seat
item.description: Krupa Antani leads Lina Godfrey by 60 votes for the third Reed Union School District board seat in Marin’s Nov. 13 count.
item.content:encoded:
Krupa Antani leads Lina Godfrey by 60 votes for the third Reed Union School District board seat in Marin’s Nov. 13 count.

By Kevin Hessel · Updated Nov. 13

UPDATE, Nov. 13: Krupa Antani widened her lead over Lina Godfrey for the third Reed Union School District board seat to 60 votes in the Marin County Elections Department’s count posted at 4:48 p.m. Nov. 13, up from 25 votes Nov. 11. Antani has 2,665 votes to Godfrey’s 2,605.

Mike Ghaffary, with 3,688 votes, and Shelby Pasarell Tsai, with 3,460, remain on track for the other two seats.

Countywide, 125,641 ballots have been counted, 72.3% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. The next county update is Nov. 17.

By Kevin Hessel · Updated Nov. 11

UPDATE, Nov. 11: Krupa Antani has moved 25 votes ahead of Lina Godfrey for the third seat on the Reed Union School District board in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 3:20 p.m. Nov. 11.

Antani had votes on 36.2% of ballots counted in the race, to Godfrey’s 35.8%, her first lead in four counts. Godfrey led on election night and by two votes Nov. 5, and the two were tied Nov. 9.

Antani and Godfrey remain tied among Tiburon voters, with 1,646 votes each. Antani’s margin comes from Belvedere, where she leads by 30 votes, while Godfrey leads by five in the Strawberry portion of the district.

The Ark projects that Mike Ghaffary, with votes on 49.9% of ballots, and Shelby Pasarell Tsai, with 46.6%, will win the other two seats.

The results are unofficial. The county’s next update is scheduled for Nov. 13.

The story below ran in the Nov. 11 print edition.

By Francisco Martinez · Nov. 3, 2026

Ghaffary, Pasarell Tsai will win Reed seats as Godfrey, Antani battle for third

Mike Ghaffary and Shelby Pasarell Tsai will win seats on the Reed Union School District board of trustees, while Lina Godfrey and fellow challenger Krupa Antani were tied for the third seat, with 1,864 votes each, in the count the county posted Nov. 9.

Ghaffary led the four-person field with votes on 49.8% of the ballots counted in the race in returns the Marin County Elections Department posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9. Pasarell Tsai had votes on 47.2% of ballots. Godfrey and Antani each had votes on 35.7% of ballots.

Those results are unofficial. Countywide, 91,634 ballots had been counted as of Nov. 9, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over missing or mismatched signatures, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them. The county’s next updates are scheduled for Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25, and state law gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

If the race for the third seat ends in a tie, the winner will be chosen by lot, under a procedure the board set before the election as state law requires, according to the district.

The top three finishers will win four-year terms that end in 2030.

Ghaffary, a venture capitalist, was appointed to the board 4-0 at a special Feb. 6 meeting to fill the seat Sherry Wangenheim left when she resigned in December 2025 with a year left on her term. His appointed term runs through early December.

Pasarell Tsai, an attorney and the board president, won her first term in 2022. Board member Afsaneh Zolfaghari did not seek a third term, so Godfrey or Antani will join the board as its newcomer.

Godfrey is a Tiburon disability-access advocate on the town’s Diversity Inclusion Task Force. Antani is a former public-school teacher with three children in the district.

“I’m very thankful that so many voters seem that they want to return me and that I’m thankful for the support,” Pasarell Tsai said.

Godfrey acknowledged on election night that results were early and commended her fellow candidates for their campaigns, saying there were “four qualified candidates for these seats.”

“I’m hopeful that we had better turnout,” she said.

“I am grateful to all the students, parents, teachers and staff who work so hard in our school district every day. Thank you to our community for continuing to support our excellent Reed Union schools,” Ghaffary said.

“I think it’s important to let the process play out,” Antani said, adding that many mail-in ballots had yet to be counted.

“Every vote matters, which is what we’re seeing in this race … so I think I’m in the mindset that we need to focus on letting this play out and getting the results in,” she said.

She said she was proud of the race and of the support for the race and for Measure O, adding that she would continue volunteering at Reed schools regardless of the results because she enjoys it.

The board race was one of two decisions facing Reed Union voters. Residents in the district, which includes Tiburon, Belvedere and east Corte Madera, also voted on Measure O, a $115 million bond measure that would fund upgrades at all three district campuses and that The Ark projects will pass.

If the bond measure holds the 55% approval it needs, the winners of the board race will join their two other colleagues in overseeing how those funds are spent. The bond is just one issue facing the Reed district. Others include continuing efforts to challenge all students academically, to balance the district budget without sacrificing student programs and to look critically at how technology is used in the classroom.

The new board will also inherit a projected $1.2 million deficit in the district’s $34.5 million budget for 2026-2027, which trustees adopted unanimously June 8. The district’s forecast shows deficits of $1.5 million in each of the next two fiscal years, and by fiscal 2029 it would fall short of the board’s own reserve policy.

Ghaffary previously said his top priorities if elected would be encouraging the district to develop responsible guidelines around technology use in the classroom, ensuring the district continues to support and challenge all students academically and continuing to plan for the district’s long-term fiscal stability.

Pasarell Tsai previously said she was focused on increasing academic rigor for all students as part of her second term. She pointed to a change the district made beginning in the 2023-2024 school year to have all seventh-grade students take accelerated math as an example of how differentiated learning can be successful. She also highlighted the board’s need to balance its budget and support district staff in what’s a “very expensive cost-of-living area.”

Antani previously said her goals included making sure the district is following its 2024-2030 strategic plan. She noted that means focusing on the whole child, including academic rigor and social-emotional learning. She also said another priority was using the district’s Local Control Accountability Plan — a state-mandated document that requires districts to outline their priorities and track student progress — as a guide to better understand whether the funds being spent for interventions and academic programs are resulting in the desired outcomes.

Godfrey said she wanted to focus on providing Reed Union students with an academically rigorous experience and increase transparency in governance. She lobbied the board to stream its meetings on Zoom to allow more people to view sessions and wants to allow for live public comment for those watching remotely.

item.title: Teacher-backed challengers win all three Tam Union board seats
item.description: Valerie Wynn, Brian Sutherland and Joy Scully Koo will win three Tamalpais Union board seats, with board President Cynthia Roenisch running fifth.
item.content:encoded:
Valerie Wynn, Brian Sutherland and Joy Scully Koo will win three Tamalpais Union board seats, with board President Cynthia Roenisch running fifth.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Three Mill Valley challengers endorsed by the district’s teachers union will win the three Tamalpais Union High School District board seats on the ballot, based on returns the county posted Nov. 9, with board President Cynthia Roenisch running fifth.

Valerie Wynn, a retired district teacher, led the seven-candidate field with votes on 48.2% of ballots counted. Brian Sutherland, an appellate and constitutional lawyer, had votes on 45.4% of ballots, and Joy Scully Koo, an engineer with an MBA, on 36.7%, according to results Marin County elections officials posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9.

Former board President Leslie Harlander, a retired civil engineer, was fourth with votes on 21.2% of ballots, just ahead of Roenisch’s 19.8% and 15.5 percentage points behind Koo. Spanish teacher Maria Sandoval had 13.9%, and Kevin Saavedra, who resigned from the board Oct. 9, had 10.9%.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The results are unofficial. The Nov. 9 count included 91,634 ballots countywide, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16.

Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over missing or mismatched signatures, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them. The county plans updates Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25, and state law gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

The district runs Redwood High School, the main public high school for Tiburon and Belvedere students, and Tamalpais High School, which serves Strawberry, along with Archie Williams High School in San Anselmo and two alternative schools. Board members are elected districtwide, so the race was on every peninsula ballot.

Taken together, peninsula voters put Sutherland first. In Tiburon’s precincts, he had votes on 41.6% of ballots to Wynn’s 39.6%, and in Belvedere 43.1% to her 36.3%. Strawberry voters put Wynn ahead, 43% to 39.9%.

Koo was third in all three communities, with 28.6% in Tiburon, 28.8% in Belvedere and 33.6% in Strawberry. Harlander ran fourth in Tiburon with 24.9%, and Roenisch was fourth in Belvedere with 20.9% and in Strawberry with 22.1%.

Ballots counted so far stood at 3,838 of 7,553 registered voters in Tiburon, 785 of 1,618 in Belvedere and 1,615 of 3,081 in Strawberry.

The third seat was open because board member Emily Uhlhorn did not seek reelection. She will finish her term and become executive director of the Tam High Foundation in January.

Saavedra stepped down the day after a judge granted a district parent a three-year civil harassment restraining order against him. His name stayed on the ballot, but he stopped campaigning and said he would not serve if elected.

Roenisch and Saavedra were first elected in 2018, the year the Marin County Office of Education ordered the district to produce a deficit-reduction plan and warned it could be insolvent as early as 2020.

Roenisch, a Corte Madera resident who teaches Advanced Placement English at Alameda High School, ran on experience, arguing at the League of Women Voters’ Sept. 28 forum that the district needed seasoned board members as budgets tighten. At a board meeting in October, parents faulted her for not publicly disciplining Saavedra, and at least one called on her to resign. She said she would not.

Most of the challengers campaigned on rebuilding trust after a string of 3-2 votes, including the June 2025 decision not to renew $250,000 in contracts with consultants who ran support programs for Black students at Tamalpais High and the April 14 bell-to-bell cellphone ban. Roenisch, Saavedra and board member Jennifer Holden formed the majority each time.

The teachers union and the Marin Democratic Party endorsed Koo, Sutherland and Wynn. A committee called Tam Union Governance Alliance supported the three while opposing Harlander, Saavedra and Roenisch, according to campaign-finance disclosures.

In the last reports before the election, covering Sept. 20 to Oct. 17, Harlander reported spending $16,010, Sutherland $8,204, Wynn $5,068 and Koo $4,786. No contributions or spending for Roenisch, Saavedra or Sandoval appeared in the county’s online filings.

The new board takes over a basic-aid district, funded mainly by local property taxes, whose enrollment fell from 5,146 students in 2020-2021 to 4,316 last school year. The district has made $3.57 million in staffing cuts since February 2025 to hold its reserves. Its Measure M parcel tax, now $560 a parcel and about 14% of a district budget of about $130 million, expires in June 2029.

The board’s minimum reserve is 17% of spending, but budget projections presented in March showed reserves dipping to about 15.5% this school year. Voters approved Measure B, a $289 million facilities bond, in 2024, eight months after a $517 million bond narrowly failed.

No Tam Union measure was on the Nov. 3 ballot. The board discussed in June whether to seek a renewal this fall but took no action before the Aug. 7 deadline. Wynn said at the forum that contract talks with the Tamalpais Federation of Teachers begin next year.

Members elected Nov. 3 take office Dec. 11, joining board members Holden and Ida Green, whose seats were not on the ballot.

item.title: Ryan, Hornbrook, Defever set to win Tiburon Town Council seats
item.description: Jack Ryan, Chuck Hornbrook and Kathleen Defever lead Faris Jafar and Alice Fredericks for three Tiburon Town Council seats in Marin’s Nov. 9 count.
item.content:encoded:
Jack Ryan, Chuck Hornbrook and Kathleen Defever lead Faris Jafar and Alice Fredericks for three Tiburon Town Council seats in Marin’s Nov. 9 count.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Jack Ryan, Chuck Hornbrook and Kathleen Defever will win the three Tiburon Town Council seats on the ballot, leading Faris Jafar and Alice Fredericks in the five-way race in the count the county posted Nov. 9.

Results as of 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9 showed Ryan leading the race with votes on 51.8% of ballots counted, followed by Hornbrook, on 51.5%, and Defever, on 43.4%. Jafar trailed with votes on 35.1% of ballots, and Fredericks had votes on 28.5%.

Because each voter could choose up to three candidates, the shares add up to more than 100%.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

Jafar and Fredericks both conceded election night.

The top three finishers will serve four-year terms until November 2030.

With Fredericks out and Mayor Jon Welner not seeking reelection, Hornbrook and Defever will join the council as its two newcomers.

The council typically accepts the certified results and rotates the mayor’s seat in December. In 2024, it accepted the results Dec. 4 and chose a new mayor the same night.

The results are unofficial. Countywide, 91,634 ballots had been counted as of Nov. 9, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16.

Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted. Voters whose ballots were challenged over missing or mismatched signatures, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them. The county’s next updates are scheduled for Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25, and state law gives it until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

Tiburon’s turnout was 84.9% in the 2024 presidential election and 71.4% in the 2022 midterm, according to certified results.

Ryan, the incumbent who first won a seat in a 2020 special election and a full term in 2022, said he was humbled by Tiburon voters’ choice in making him the leading vote-getter and looked forward to the new term.

“We’re going to have at least one new councilmember, and I’m excited to work with the new council in the new year,” he added.

Hornbrook, a Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission member who ran unsuccessfully in 2024, said he looked forward to addressing issues he heard on the campaign trail, estimating he knocked on some 900 doors. In a Nov. 6 statement to The Ark, he said he would focus on traffic, community vibrancy and town accountability.

He said he was excited to be “getting to work and helping deliver what the people of Tiburon want to get done.”

Defever, a Planning Commission member who ran unsuccessfully for the council in 2020 and 2021, said she had just seen the results when The Ark contacted her and was thrilled. The results were “something I’ve been looking forward to,” she said.

“I’m excited to have the voters’ support, and I cannot wait to get to work and get some of the issues I’ve heard about on the campaign trail addressed,” Defever said.

“I think Tiburon’s decided pretty decisively who they wanted, and I’m excited to work with everybody on all the initiatives we talked about during the campaign,” Jafar said. “To the extent that I can help with the policy initiatives we talked during the campaign, I’m happy to lend a hand.”

Fredericks, the longest-serving councilmember in Tiburon’s history, said she would now consider her next volunteer options.

“I would like to congratulate the people who now sit on the council,” Fredericks said. “It’s going to be very exciting.”

Ryan, Hornbrook and Defever will serve on a council facing calls for more financial transparency after delayed year-end audits and a budgeting process that did not include up-to-date actual spending figures from the prior year, including for the current fiscal year 2026-2027. All five candidates backed an independent finance committee like Belvedere’s.

Those financial concerns extend to new revenue sources. Town Manager Greg Chanis told councilmembers May 20 that Tiburon must explore how to pay for park improvements, a longstanding upgrade of the Public Works Department’s corporation yard and improvements identified in the town’s traffic study, adopted in May.

Housing remains a central issue. The state Department of Housing and Community Development can review Tiburon’s housing element at midcycle as soon as summer 2027, examining whether the town is following through on the housing programs it has committed to.

Tiburon was allocated 639 units as part of its 2023-2031 housing-element cycle. Although the town needs only to identify where the units can be built, falling short in the review could trigger consequences.

Town officials previously indicated the most severe consequences would make the town ineligible for state funding, expose it to sanctions from the state Attorney General’s Office and activate the “builder’s remedy,” under which developers could build regardless of local zoning restrictions.

At the center of the housing discussion is a 127-unit plan for three downtown Tiburon sites owned by A&C Ventures. The company announced the plan Oct. 22; its 127 units would cover nearly 20% of the town’s housing allocation.

The new council will also inherit unsettled questions on parks and police cameras. The town has not decided how to pay for a planned park at the former sanitation ponds site near McKegney Green, projected to cost $3.7 million to build, and the earliest voters could approve a tax or bond for it is November 2028.

All five candidates said they were open to a public hearing on the town’s Flock license-plate cameras, a debate that had not reached a council agenda as of Election Day.

Hornbrook, a vocal advocate for more fiscal transparency, has pledged to bring the creation of a finance committee to a council vote within his first 90 days in office. On town revenue, he wants to examine how the town spends its money and cut costs where needed before considering a bond measure or sales-tax increase.

On housing, Hornbrook supports talking with other agencies, such as the Reed Union School District, to explore workforce-housing solutions. He said the town should work with the state mandates as written; challenging them, he said, can result in even less local control.

Ryan also supports an independent finance committee to help the council analyze town revenues and expenditures and plan ahead. He said the town should communicate its finances better, and he has said the word “transparency” in a government context results in “an inference or an implication that something’s being hidden.”

Ryan said he wanted to plan the town’s long-term spending before deciding how to raise money, but he said raising the town’s sales tax by half a cent is an option to close gaps for projects. On housing, Ryan considered A&C Ventures’ efforts to have the greatest effect on how the town thinks about its housing element.

Defever also supports more financial transparency and said councilmembers should listen to residents who ask for more information. She said she wanted to examine the town budget more closely to figure out how Tiburon could add revenue sources, but she has said there are ways Tiburon can cut its spending, such as on litigation, before exploring new revenue.

Defever has criticized state housing mandates, describing their implementation as “one size fits all.” She previously said that while the town must follow state law, Tiburon should also “try to come up with some alternative strategies to maintain Tiburon for the beautiful attributes that it has.”

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The next results updates are scheduled for Nov. 11, 13, 17, 20 and 25. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16. Voters whose ballots were challenged over missing or mismatched signatures, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them. State law gives Marin County until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

Reed Union board President Shelby Pasarell Tsai, who was also on the ballot for reelection, said on election night that “early returns look good” and that she was feeling “hopefully optimistic” for the district.

Pasarell Tsai said she was “really looking forward to community recognizing the importance of strong and vibrant schools, and it shows that our community really does value the schools.”

The tax would be levied on properties in the district, which includes Tiburon, Belvedere and east Corte Madera, beginning in fiscal year 2027-2028, when the district expects the rate to peak at $30 per $100,000 of assessed value. That works out to $300 a year for every $1 million of assessed value.

The district estimates the rate would average $26.63 per $100,000 over the life of the bonds, with the tax collected for the last time in fiscal 2060-2061. The levy would raise about $6.2 million a year, according to the ballot question, and the district’s tax rate statement estimates that repaying the full $115 million would cost $213 million in principal and interest.

Property owners in the district already pay a combined rate of about $21.60 per $100,000 of assessed value for two earlier Reed school bonds: a $38 million bond approved in 2001 that ends in 2028 and a $13 million bond that ends in 2031, according to district consultant Capital Finance Group.

The district’s current bond rate is the third lowest among 12 elementary school districts in Marin, according to figures presented to the board June 2. With Measure O, its rate would still fall in the middle range of comparable districts.

No argument against Measure O was filed with the Marin County Elections Department.

The district’s board voted unanimously June 8 to put the measure on the ballot. The district will set priorities for the money using its long-range facilities plan, begun in spring 2022 and completed in 2024 to guide building projects at the three campuses over the next 10-15 years.

Pasarell Tsai said before the election that $115 million falls short of the district’s needs and that the district has no intention of bringing a second bond measure to voters.

School districts in California usually turn to bond measures to pay for repairs, renovations and new construction because they receive no dedicated funding for facilities upkeep. A bond functions as a loan taken out by the school district that property owners pay back through increased property taxes.

No bond money can be used for teacher or administrator salaries, and the measure requires a citizens’ oversight committee and annual independent audits. The measure’s text also says the money must be spent on the district’s schools and cannot be taken by the state or county.

Needs across the district include replacing portable classrooms and installing air conditioning in all rooms on all three campuses.

Other districtwide work includes upgrading failing clay-pipe plumbing, repairing leaking roofs, removing asbestos and mold from aging buildings and making campuses more accessible than the Americans with Disabilities Act requires.

At Bel Aire Elementary School, identified improvements include installing heaters in three buildings, repaving the lower playground and creating shade for the lunch area.

At Reed Elementary School, other high-priority work includes replacing roofs over the administration building, building a covered lunch area and replacing old walkways.

And at Del Mar Middle School, improvements include repaving the playground, fixing concrete and asphalt, replacing stairs from the field to the street and redoing the track.

item.title: Tiburon’s Marilyn Nemzer wins new term on Marin Board of Education
item.description: Marilyn Nemzer had 70.3% of the vote over fellow Tiburon resident Avery Lieberman for the Marin County Board of Education seat covering the peninsula.
item.content:encoded:
Marilyn Nemzer had 70.3% of the vote over fellow Tiburon resident Avery Lieberman for the Marin County Board of Education seat covering the peninsula.

Updated Nov. 9 with the county’s 3:11 p.m. count.

Tiburon resident Marilyn Nemzer will win another four years on the Marin County Board of Education over a challenger backed by one of her board colleagues.

Nemzer had 70.3% of the vote to 29.7% for challenger and fellow Tiburon resident Avery Lieberman in county results posted at 3:11 p.m. Nov. 9, the latest available at The Ark’s press time.

The Trustee Area 5 seat covers all of Tiburon, Belvedere and Strawberry as well as Corte Madera and Larkspur. The Reed Union School District lies entirely within its boundaries. The winner will serve a four-year term ending in November 2030.

Complete coverage: thearknewspaper.com/election2026

Live results: thearknewspaper.com/election2026/results

The results are unofficial. As of Nov. 9, the county had counted 91,634 ballots, about 52.7% of Marin’s 173,804 registered voters. Mailed ballots postmarked by Election Day had until Nov. 10 to arrive and still be counted.

The next results updates are scheduled for Nov. 11, as well as Nov. 13, 17, 20 and 25. State law requires the county to finish counting most ballots by Nov. 16. Voters whose ballots were challenged over missing or mismatched signatures, 2,369 in Marin as of Nov. 5, have until 5 p.m. Nov. 25 to fix them. State law gives Marin County until Dec. 3 to certify the results.

Registrar of Voters Natalie Adona said the county expects to finish counting most ballots by the Nov. 16 deadline and aims to certify the results before Thanksgiving.

Nemzer said on election night that she was relieved and happy with the early results and that being elected is a special feeling.

“I just love being involved in what we do on the board, and I’m just really, really happy that it looks like I will have a chance to continue,” Nemzer said in a phone interview.

Lieberman declined to comment on the results.

The Marin County Board of Education provides citizen oversight of educational programs and services run by the Marin County Office of Education. It works with the voter-elected county superintendent of schools to set county-office priorities.

Its duties include adopting or rejecting, but not modifying, the elected superintendent’s proposed budget; setting the superintendent’s salary; hearing appeals of student expulsions or denied interdistrict transfer requests; and maintaining positive relationships with the county’s 17 school districts.

Nemzer, 84, has represented the Tiburon Peninsula on the board since 2001 and sought a seventh term. Her key priorities include maintaining the county Office of Education’s long-term programs, including outdoor education at Walker Creek Ranch and Career Technical Education, and expanding collaboration among districts to share services and cut costs.

Lieberman, 65, a former assistant professor of dentistry, has lived in Tiburon for 31 years.

The race was the first contested election for the seat in at least 13 years. Nemzer was the only candidate to file in 2013, and no challenger emerged in 2018 or 2022.

Nemzer’s race became a proxy for existing tensions on the school board between her and board member Nancy McCarthy, who encouraged Lieberman to run and who has clashed repeatedly with her colleagues on the board.

Lieberman was one of three challengers seeking to unseat incumbents on the seven-member board, and he said McCarthy also recruited another of them, The Ark reported in September.

McCarthy — who has drawn criticism from her colleagues in recorded meetings, including claims that she has created a toxic environment during her tenure — financially supported a committee, Educate Our Children, that spent against Nemzer and fellow incumbent Curtis Robinson, who also sought reelection. Robinson will win his race to represent Sausalito and part of Mill Valley.

McCarthy has criticized Nemzer for accepting county-paid health benefits, which Lieberman said he would not accept if elected. Nemzer has defended the benefit, saying the option to receive health coverage allows people from lower-income backgrounds to seek the office.

Lieberman’s social-media posts have also drawn accusations of bigotry. He sued the University of California in November 2020, alleging he was laid off from his job as an assistant clinical professor at its San Francisco dental school and publicly branded a racist over posts on his personal Facebook page. The parties settled the suit in October 2024, with no admission of wrongdoing and no allegations tested at trial.

In one post, Lieberman wrote that saying “all lives matter” was “now considered to be the ‘go-to response from a racist.’” He also commented “So true!” on another user’s post invoking slavery, Jim Crow and reparations. Lieberman deleted the “all lives matter” post and apologized publicly after a colleague told him students had been hurt by it, according to his complaint. In a deposition, Lieberman acknowledged a reader could construe his agreement with the latter post as racist.

The dispute began in June 2020, days after George Floyd’s murder in Minneapolis. A student complained that Lieberman’s posts were offensive, according to court filings. A faculty member relayed the student’s words in an email quoted in the case: “Apparently this is how he feels about people of my skin color.” The student said Lieberman had since deleted “a lot of the racial posts.”

More recently, in April, Lieberman wrote Facebook posts directed at Muslims as a group.

In an April 19 post, Lieberman shared a Breitbart story headlined “North London Synagogue ‘Firebombed’ in Latest Anti-Jewish Attack.” Above the link he wrote: “For those of you who favor open borders and unelected judges (Obama appointees) who block efforts to deport violent hate filled Muslims.”

In an April 17 post, Lieberman shared a message from conservative commentator David J. Harris Jr. paraphrasing Catholic Bishop Athanasius Schneider: “They are not refugees, they are invaders who want to Islamize Europe. They want to destroy historical culture in Europe.” Harris asked, “Thoughts?” Lieberman answered, “And they’ve succeeded.”

In September, Lieberman defended the posts and said he was not referring to all Muslims.

“Most are peaceful and tolerant but a small percentage aren’t,” he wrote. Lieberman, who is Jewish, added that he was concerned about rising antisemitism worldwide and feels an obligation to speak up against attacks on Jews.

Lieberman said those who “try to label me as racist or hateful” over the posts should recognize that he has been a victim of hate himself. He said he would stand up for people of all races and religions.

“I support diversity, equity and inclusion, but only when applied to everyone, not just certain groups,” he wrote.

item.title: Belvedere’s Lava House lots are listed for $30 million
item.description: The four vacant Belvedere Avenue lots where Jerry Ganz spent two decades fighting to build, known as the Lava House site, are for sale as one package for $30 million.
item.content:encoded:
The four vacant Belvedere Avenue lots where Jerry Ganz spent two decades fighting to build, known as the Lava House site, are for sale as one package for $30 million.

The four vacant Belvedere Avenue lots where the late seat-belt manufacturer Jerry Ganz spent two decades fighting to build, the site of the ruin known locally as the Lava House, are for sale as one package for $30 million.

The parcels at 399, 401, 415 and 419 Belvedere Ave. total about 2.75 acres above Richardson Bay, with views of the Golden Gate Bridge, the San Francisco skyline and Mount Tamalpais. The Sarkissian Bullock Team of Golden Gate Sotheby’s International Realty listed the land in mid-September and publicized it in an Oct. 29 news release.

The lots will not be sold separately, said Kevin Daniel Dwyer, the brokerage’s chief marketing officer. The site remains fenced, and showings are limited to “vetted, qualified buyers,” whom the agents walk through the property themselves, he said.

The listing lands as a new wave of artificial-intelligence wealth builds around the bay. San Francisco-based Anthropic filed Oct. 26 to go public, with a listing expected as soon as mid-November, and designer Jony Ive, whose AI-device startup OpenAI bought for $6.5 billion in 2025, paid $43.5 million last year for Belvedere’s Locksley Hall.

Dwyer pointed to the same money.

“The influx of wealth and the emerging affluent in the S.F. Bay Area from the AI and tech sectors presents a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for a qualified buyer,” he said in an email.

County records show 399, 401 and 415 are held by Belvedere 401 LLC, which took title in 2020 from the family’s 401 Belvedere Corp., and 419 by the Peggy Homestead Trust, a trust for Ganz’s daughter, Peggy. Stan Beainy, a longtime trustee for the family, died in December, and Ganz has also died, Dwyer said. The family is not available for comment, he said.

The lots are zoned R-15, Belvedere’s single-family district for parcels of at least 15,000 square feet. On any one lot, a home’s floor area may not exceed 33% of the lot or 4,850 square feet, whichever is less, though the Planning Commission can allow a larger house if it finds the lot has unusual features that lessen the impact of a bigger house, the extra space would not significantly block neighbors’ views or substantially reduce their privacy, and the house is appropriate in mass and bulk.

An architect the listing agents consulted expects the size of these lots to help.

“Because the lots are larger than the minimum requirement, there is a reasonable chance that an exception to total floor area for a larger home would be approved, though it is not guaranteed,” David Kotzebue of David Kotzebue Architecture said in a statement provided by the agents.

State law also lets each lot carry more than one home. A single-family lot can add an accessory dwelling unit inside the house or an existing accessory structure, a detached unit and a junior unit of up to 500 square feet carved from the home, for as many as four homes per lot, or 16 across the property.

Belvedere caps a standard detached unit at 850 square feet, or 1,000 square feet with two bedrooms. Under the city’s size bonus, adopted in 2025, an owner who agrees to keep the rent affordable to low- or very-low-income households can build up to 1,000 square feet, or 1,200 with two or more bedrooms.

Belvedere’s housing element, the state-mandated plan that won certification in February, counts the four lots as one future home each, all at above-moderate income levels. If a buyer combines them for fewer homes, the state’s no-net-loss law can require the city to show capacity for the difference elsewhere.

Planning and Building Director Rebecca Markwick said the city would work with its housing attorney to determine how to prevent a net loss. No applications or approvals are active on the lots, she said, and any project would need a geotechnical report and approval from the Bay Conservation and Development Commission, the same as any new construction on a Belvedere Island hillside.

Marin’s record home sale remains Locksley Hall at 440 Golden Gate Ave., which sold for $47.5 million in 2015. Ive’s 2025 purchase was part of a private, four-home, $73 million deal, and an estate at 20 Crest Road was listed in May at $50 million.

For land, the agents point to the $42.1 million the Trust for Public Land paid in 2024 for Easton Point, the 110-acre Martha property on the Tiburon Ridge, which they call the most expensive land sale in Marin County history.

Two of the four Belvedere Avenue lots have sold before. In May 2015, 401 Belvedere Corp. and the Peggy Homestead Trust sold 415 and 419 for $8.65 million to a trust of Howard R. King, and the sellers carried a $6.06 million loan, county records show. In October 2017, the King trust deeded both lots back in lieu of foreclosure, with about $6.1 million still owed.

Dwyer said his team was not involved in that transaction.

Ganz, who made his fortune manufacturing seat belts in Chicago, began buying land on the Belvedere shoreline in 1972 and sought a 30,000-square-foot mansion that the city denied. He sued Belvedere twice, alleging a conspiracy, in suits that dragged on for nearly two decades. He lost one and won the other.

In 1986, he also bought the neighboring lot at 425 Belvedere Ave. from the widow of casino owner Bill Harrah and tore down the Harrahs’ home. The city approved a 16,000-square-foot glass house there in 1992, but work stopped after a landslide about two years later, and the house was never built.

Next door, Ganz’s crews had covered the slopes in lava rock, which The Ark reported was imported from Hawaii. Local lore holds it was barged in from the islands and cursed, after the legend that taking lava rock from Hawaii angers Pele, goddess of fire and volcanoes, and that the curse brought the landslides and the fire that later burned part of the property.

In the early 1990s, police answered a report of “satanic rituals” on the property; no one was arrested. In 1996, a fire that authorities said was possibly arson burned a garage and caretaker’s unit, and in 2004 a house at 401 was torn down, leaving its foundation and the lava rock behind.

Ganz walked away from 425 in 2008, when real-estate developer Jeff Paster bought it. Paster won approval in 2009 for a roughly 15,500-square-foot home there, opened it as a Marin Designers Showcase house and listed it at $45 million. It sold in September 2013 for $24.5 million, then a Marin record.

The rest of the land sat for decades as a maze of empty pools, grottoes and crumbling stairways, a magnet for teenagers and a recurring call for Belvedere police.

In December 2018, the Planning Commission voted 5-0, with commissioners Jim Lynch and Larry Stoehr absent, to approve a $600,000 cleanup. Crews working from March through December 2019 used a remote-controlled demolition robot and hauled about 500 to 600 cubic yards of rock and debris away by barge.

“Kids were cutting through the fence and going down on the property; we found drug paraphernalia. People were going down there and starting fires,” Beainy said as the work began.

A hog-wire fence went up under a condition that it stay only until the property is sold and a new project comes forward.

item.title: Strawberry swimmer completes 900-mile journey down California coast
item.description: Strawberry resident Catherine Breed finished a roughly 900-mile swim down the California coast Oct. 19, the first person to swim the state’s length, pending ratification.
item.content:encoded:
Strawberry resident Catherine Breed finished a roughly 900-mile swim down the California coast Oct. 19, the first person to swim the state’s length, pending ratification.

On her drive home to Marin from San Diego on Oct. 27, Strawberry resident Catherine Breed, a 33-year-old open-water swimmer, saw the California coastline from the road and took stock of her most recent odyssey.

“Oh my gosh,” Breed recalled thinking to herself. “I swam all of that.”

Breed the week before completed a roughly 900-mile journey called “Swim California,” navigating her way from the Oregon border all the way down to Mexico. She began July 1 and swam the coast in daily stages from a support sailboat over 111 days, 18 of them lost to weather and rest. When she finished her swim Oct. 19, Breed became the first person to swim the length of the Golden State, pending ratification by the World Open Water Swimming Association.
